opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a lot of excitement right now, and a lot of money going into humanoid robots and robotics startups, but the dirty secret of the industry is that most of these companies don't really know how to make their robots smart enough to be generally useful. They can make them do impressive demos, often teleoperated or trained for a very specific task, but we're still very far from a robot that you can put in a new environment and have it figure out what to do.

And the reason is something I've been saying for years: we don't have AI systems that understand the physical world. Large language models are very good at manipulating language, but language is not where most of intelligence is. A four-year-old child has seen more data through vision than the biggest LLM has been trained on in text. A house cat understands the physical world, can plan complex actions, and we can't reproduce that with robots. That's the Moravec paradox, still very much with us.

So what's missing is what I call world models: systems that learn, mostly from observation like video, how the world works, so they can predict the consequences of their actions and plan a sequence of actions to accomplish a goal. That's what architectures like JEPA are about: predicting in an abstract representation space rather than trying to predict every pixel, because the world is largely unpredictable at the pixel level.

Once we have that, and I think we'll see significant progress over the next few years, robotics will take off, because the bottleneck isn't really the hardware anymore. The hardware is getting cheaper and quite good. The bottleneck is the intelligence. So, reliably useful in narrow settings like factories and warehouses, that's happening already. Reliably useful in your home, doing whatever you ask? That requires a new paradigm in AI, and I'd say we're not going to get there just by scaling up current approaches. It's probably a matter of years, maybe the next decade, but it won't come from LLMs.

r001.rationale: The response mentions teleoperated demos and robots trained for specific tasks, but does not identify imitation learning as the approach or say it is the only approach companies currently know for reliable performance.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest.

Well, I think there's a bit of a disconnect right now between the hype and the reality. You see all these very impressive demos, humanoid robots dancing, folding laundry, and people get the impression that we're basically there. We're not there.

The hardware has actually become quite good. The motors, the actuators, the sensors, the cost is coming down. That's not the bottleneck anymore. The bottleneck is the intelligence. For a robot to be reliably useful in an unstructured environment, like your kitchen or a hospital, it needs to understand how the physical world works. It needs a world model. It needs to be able to predict what's going to happen if it pushes this object, or grabs that handle, or steps on that surface. And it needs to plan, to anticipate the consequences of a sequence of actions before taking them. We don't know how to do that yet, not at the level a cat or a ten-year-old does.

What companies are doing today is essentially collecting enormous amounts of teleoperation data and training policies by imitation. And that works for a narrow set of tasks, in a narrow set of conditions. But it doesn't generalize. The moment the situation deviates a bit from the training distribution, the robot does something stupid. And the big difference with LLMs is that in the real world, you can't just make errors and have the user ignore them. If the robot breaks a glass or falls down the stairs, that's a real cost. So reliability is really the whole game, and reliability requires understanding, not just pattern matching on trajectories.

So my view is that in factories, in warehouses, in controlled settings, we'll see useful robots fairly soon, some already exist. But the general-purpose robot in the home that you can ask to do arbitrary things, that requires scientific breakthroughs that haven't happened yet. I'd say that's a decade, maybe more. Which is why I keep saying the next decade might be the decade of robotics, in the sense that this is where the interesting problems are, and where progress in AI will be driven, by systems that actually have to deal with the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response says companies currently train policies by imitation and that this works for a narrow set of tasks and conditions. It does not identify imitation learning as the only approach companies know for achieving reliable performance.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends very much on what you mean by useful. In a factory, where you can control the environment, robots are already useful. But a robot that you can put in an unfamiliar kitchen and ask to clear the table—that’s a much harder problem.

What’s missing is not just better hardware. It’s the ability to understand the physical world, predict the consequences of actions, and plan. A robot needs to know that if it pulls a plate out from under a glass, something bad might happen, without having to try that thousands of times.

We have systems that can learn impressive behaviors from demonstrations. The difficulty is getting them to work reliably when something changes: the object is different, someone moves a chair, or the robot makes a mistake and has to recover. A successful demonstration and a useful product are very different things.

So I would expect useful robots in fairly constrained settings first. For general-purpose household robots, I think we still need substantial advances in learning and world models. I wouldn’t put a precise date on that.

r001.rationale: The response mentions learning behaviors from demonstrations, but does not identify imitation learning for a small set of tasks as the only approach robotics companies currently know for reliable performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends very much on what you mean by useful. In a controlled environment, doing a repetitive task, robots are already useful. But if you want a robot that can help you around the house, deal with unfamiliar objects, and recover when something unexpected happens, we’re still missing some important ingredients.

The big difficulty is that robots don’t have the common sense that allows an animal to understand the physical world. A cat can look at a situation and have a pretty good idea of what will happen if it jumps or pushes something. We don’t have systems with that level of understanding and planning yet.

There’s exciting progress in learning from demonstrations. But collecting enough demonstrations to cover every situation is not going to work. You need systems that learn models of the world, predict the consequences of their actions, and use those predictions to plan. I’m optimistic we’ll make progress on that, but I wouldn’t give you a precise date for a reliable general-purpose household robot.

r001.rationale: The response mentions learning from demonstrations and robots working on repetitive tasks, but does not identify imitation learning for a small set of tasks as the only approach robotics companies currently know for reliable performance.
